equation_request.abstract:
We present a quantum Viterbi algorithm (QVA) with better than classical performance under certain conditions. In this paper the proposed algorithm is applied to decoding classical convolutional codes, for instance; large constraint length $Q$ and short decode frames $N$. Other applications of the classical Viterbi algorithm where $Q$ is large (e.g. speech processing) could experience significant speedup with the QVA. The QVA exploits the fact that the decoding trellis is similar to the butterfly diagram of the fast Fourier transform, with its corresponding fast quantum algorithm. The tensor-product structure of the butterfly diagram corresponds to a quantum superposition that we show can be efficiently prepared. The quantum speedup is possible because the performance of the QVA depends on the fanout (number of possible transitions from any given state in the hidden Markov model) which is in general much less than $Q$. The QVA constructs a superposition of states which correspond to all legal paths through the decoding lattice, with phase a function of the probability of the path being taken given received data. A specialized amplitude amplification procedure is applied one or more times to recover a superposition where the most probable path has a high probability of being measured.

**Key words and phrases:**

Viterbi Algorithm and Hidden Markov Model and Convolutional Code and Tensor-Product Structure and Butterfly Diagram and Amplitude Amplification and Quantum Function Optimum Finding

specification.problem: Maximum-likelihood (Viterbi) decoding of a binary convolutional code: given a received noisy word y of N frames, find the input sequence x (equivalently the legal trellis path) that maximises P(y|x). The abstract proposes a quantum Viterbi algorithm (QVA) that prepares a superposition over all legal trellis paths with a probability-dependent phase and then applies a specialised amplitude-amplification / quantum optimum-finding procedure so that the most probable path is measured with high probability.
specification.reconstruction_scope: No experiment scope was supplied, so one smallest useful construction is chosen (assumption): a rate-1/2, memory-1 (constraint length Q=2, fanout 2) binary convolutional code, hard-decision BSC channel, N=3 decode frames, trellis starting in the zero state. In this fanout-2 setting every input bit string x in {0,1}^N is a legal path, so the 'tensor-product' path superposition is H^{\otimes N}. The path metric is the Hamming distance d(x) between y and the codeword, which is an affine function of log P(y|x). Because the paper's specialised amplitude-amplification procedure is not described in the abstract, the baseline uses the standard Durr-Hoyer threshold-oracle minimum finding (Grover iterations) as a stand-in. A concrete received word y=(11,01,11) is fixed so that the unique ML path is x=101 with d=1. Outside scope: large-Q codes, general HMMs with fanout-restricted transition structure, the explicit butterfly/FFT-style preparation of constrained path superpositions, the paper's actual phase function and specialised amplification, and any complexity/speedup claims.

symbols.meaning: number of decode frames (trellis depth); instance value N=3
constraint length of the convolutional code; instance value Q=2 (memory 1, 2 trellis states)
input (information) bit sequence; indexes a legal trellis path; x_0:=0 is the initial encoder state
pair of code bits emitted at frame t
received hard-decision word, y_t in {0,1}^2; instance y=(11,01,11)
crossover probability of the binary symmetric channel
path metric: Hamming distance between y and the codeword of x
current threshold in the minimum-finding loop
unspecified phase function of the path probability used by the paper's QVA
threshold phase oracle marking paths with d(x)<T
metric register width, m=\lceil\log_2(2N+1)\rceil; instance m=3

equations.label: Tensor-product superposition over all legal paths
equations.description: Uniform superposition over all input sequences; for a fanout-2 trellis with unconstrained inputs every x is a legal path, so the path superposition factorises as a tensor product of single-qubit states.
equations.abstract_quote: The tensor-product structure of the butterfly diagram corresponds to a quantum superposition that we show can be efficiently prepared.
equations.justification: The abstract claims the legal-path superposition has tensor-product structure and is efficiently preparable; for the chosen fanout-2 instance this is exactly H^{\otimes N}. The general constrained-HMM preparation is not reconstructed.
assumptions: Fanout 2 with every input sequence legal (binary convolutional code, zero initial state).
Qubit t of the path register holds x_t; register ordering x_1 is the most significant / leftmost qubit.

equations.label: Trellis / encoder for the Q=2 rate-1/2 instance
equations.latex: c_t^{(1)} = x_t,\qquad c_t^{(2)} = x_t \oplus x_{t-1},\qquad x_0 = 0,\quad t=1,\dots,N
equations.description: Memory-1 convolutional encoder (generators (1, 1+D)); the trellis state at time t is x_t and each state has fanout 2.
equations.justification: A concrete smallest nontrivial convolutional code is needed to make the metric computable; this specific code is not given in the abstract.

equations.label: Path metric and its relation to path probability (BSC)
equations.description: Hamming-distance path metric; on a memoryless BSC the log-likelihood is an exactly affine, strictly decreasing function of d(x), so the most probable path is the minimum-metric path. For the instance y=(11,01,11), d(101)=1 is the unique minimum.
equations.justification: Standard Viterbi/ML decoding relation for hard-decision BSC; needed to connect 'probability of the path' in the abstract to a computable integer metric.

equations.label: Phase-encoded path superposition (paper's construction, form unknown)
equations.latex: |\psi_\varphi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^N}}\sum_{x} e^{\,i\,\varphi\left(P(y\mid x)\right)}|x\rangle,\qquad \text{reversible metric computation: } U_d|x\rangle|0\rangle^{\otimes m} = |x\rangle|d(x)\rangle
equations.description: The abstract states that each legal path carries a phase that is a function of its posterior/likelihood; the specific function \varphi is not given. The baseline realises the needed information instead by reversibly computing d(x) into an m-qubit metric register (first equality is the abstract's claim; second is the baseline substitute).
equations.abstract_quote: with phase a function of the probability of the path being taken given received data
equations.justification: Directly paraphrases the abstract's description of the constructed superposition; the exact \varphi and its use in the specialised amplification are unknown, so the baseline uses a computed-metric register.
assumptions: \varphi is unspecified; the baseline does not rely on it.
U_d is a reversible arithmetic circuit computing eq_3 from eq_2 (XOR and popcount adders).

equations.label: Threshold marking oracle
equations.description: Phase oracle that flips the sign of every path whose metric is strictly below the current threshold; implemented by computing d(x), applying a comparator-controlled phase, and uncomputing.
equations.justification: Standard construction for Durr-Hoyer quantum minimum finding; used as a stand-in for the paper's 'specialized amplitude amplification procedure', which the abstract does not specify.
assumptions: C_{<T} is a comparator phase gate acting on the metric register (phase kickback on an ancilla).

equations.label: Amplitude-amplification iterate and success probability
equations.description: Grover iterate with the uniform-superposition reflection; after k iterations the probability of measuring a path with metric below T is sin^2((2k+1)theta_T). For the instance (N=3, T=2, one marked path) k=2 gives P_succ = sin^2(5 asin(1/sqrt 8)) ~ 0.945.
equations.justification: Standard amplitude amplification; the abstract only states that a specialised procedure is applied 'one or more times' to boost the most probable path, consistent with an iterative minimum-finding loop.
assumptions: Number of marked paths unknown in general; Durr-Hoyer randomised iteration counts (or exponential search) handle this.
The paper's specialised procedure may differ materially from this generic iterate.

registers.name: path
registers.role: Holds the input bit sequence x; one qubit per frame, qubit t = x_t; indexes the legal trellis path

registers.name: metric
registers.role: Reversibly computed Hamming-distance metric d(x) in binary (unsigned, little-endian assumed)

registers.name: flag
registers.role: Comparator output / phase-kickback ancilla for the threshold test d(x) < T

specification.initial_state: |0\rangle^{\otimes N}_{\text{path}} \otimes |0\rangle^{\otimes m}_{\text{metric}} \otimes |-\rangle_{\text{flag}} (flag prepared as (|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2} for phase kickback)

steps.description: Prepare the tensor-product superposition over all legal trellis paths by applying H to every path qubit.
Classically fix the received word y (instance y=(11,01,11)) and the encoder/trellis map; initialise threshold T (e.g. T = 2N+1, or T = d(x_r)+? from a random classical path x_r as in Durr-Hoyer).
Apply the threshold oracle: compute d(x) into the metric register with U_d, apply the comparator phase for d(x) < T via the flag ancilla, and uncompute U_d.

Apply the reflection about |psi_0> (H^{\otimes N}, phase flip on |0...0>, H^{\otimes N}) to complete one Grover iterate G_T; repeat k times with k chosen for the (possibly unknown) number of marked paths.
Measure the path register, obtain candidate x'; classically compute d(x'); if d(x') < T set T = d(x') and repeat from step 1 ('applied one or more times'), otherwise stop.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of the N-qubit path register yielding a candidate input sequence x'. The metric register is returned to |0...0> by uncomputation and need not be measured.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Compute d(x') classically (eq_3); keep the best candidate and update the threshold T; repeat the quantum loop until the threshold stops decreasing or an iteration budget is exhausted. Output x̂ = best candidate as the decoded information bits (instance: expected x̂ = 101 with d=1).
assumptions: No experiment scope was given; a smallest useful instance was chosen: Q=2, rate-1/2, generators (1, 1+D), N=3, zero initial state, hard-decision BSC, received word y=(11,01,11).

In this fanout-2 instance all 2^N input sequences are legal paths, so the legal-path superposition is exactly H^{\otimes N}; the paper's general butterfly/tensor-product preparation for constrained HMMs is not reconstructed.

The paper's 'specialized amplitude amplification procedure' and the phase function \varphi are unknown; the baseline substitutes standard Durr-Hoyer threshold-oracle minimum finding with a reversibly computed metric register.
Metric register is unsigned binary of width ceil(log2(2N+1)); no modular wrap-around occurs since d(x) <= 2N.
missing_information: Exact phase function \varphi relating path probability to the phase of each path amplitude, and how that phase is consumed by the amplification procedure.
Definition of the 'specialized amplitude amplification procedure' and its iteration schedule ('one or more times').
How the trellis/butterfly tensor-product structure is used to prepare the superposition over legal paths for general fanout and constrained HMM transition structure (large Q, non-binary inputs).
Conditions under which the claimed better-than-classical performance holds (dependence on fanout, Q, N) and the asserted complexity.
Treatment of soft-decision metrics / general HMM emission probabilities (only hard-decision Hamming metric is used here).
Termination/tail-biting conventions for the trellis and the final encoder state.
